the-name.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **त्वष्टृ**. Etymologically it means "'The Fashioner, the Maker' (from tvaṣ, to form), the divine craftsman"[^1].

The ASCII form *tvastr* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Tvaṣṭṛ** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the underdots of ṣ, ṭ, and ṛ — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Same letter
- **v** → **v** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter
- **s** → **ṣ** — Script-specific diacritic
- **t** → **ṭ** — Script-specific diacritic
- **r** → **ṛ** — Script-specific diacritic

The project holds the domain **tvaṣṭṛ.com** (xn--tva-u7ytb8c.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

overview.body:
**Tvaṣṭṛ** (*tvastr*) — The Architect of the Gods — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Craft, Making, Form". The name means "'The Fashioner, the Maker' (from tvaṣ, to form), the divine craftsman"[^1].

Tvaṣṭṛ is the divine smith of the Ṛgveda: maker of Indra's thunderbolt, shaper of the soma cup, fashioner of wombs and forms — and the father whose grief over his slain son produced the greatest monster of Vedic myth.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Tvaṣṭṛ** and serves its temple at [tvaṣṭṛ.com](https://xn--tva-u7ytb8c.com). The restoration preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the underdots of ṣ, ṭ, and ṛ — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *tvastr* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **त्वष्टृ**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *tvaṣṭṛ*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- त्व = tva
- ष = ṣa
- टृ = ṭṛ (vocalic ṛ)
- tvaṣṭṛ is the divine craftsman who shapes the forms of the gods

Written त्वष्टृ in Devanagari: tva with its conjunct, ṣa with the retroflex dot, and tṛ with the vocalic ṛ sign. The same root family gives takṣan, the carpenter — the god's name and the village craft are one word apart.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

domains.body:
Tvaṣṭṛ is the divine smith of the Ṛgveda: maker of Indra's thunderbolt, shaper of the soma cup, fashioner of wombs and forms — and the father whose grief over his slain son produced the greatest monster of Vedic myth.[^1]

### The Vajra

He forged Indra's thunderbolt — the weapon that split the dragon's fortress.

### Vṛtra's Father

In grief he shaped the avenger: Vṛtra, born to kill Indra, by the rite gone wrong.

### Viśvarūpa

His three-headed son, the gods' priest, slain by Indra — the wound that drove the forge.

### The Soma Cup

He fashioned the very cup from which the gods drink immortality.

sources.citation: Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Tvaṣṭṛ concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The axe and chisel** — The fashioner's tools — form struck from the formless
- **The cup** — The soma vessel — liturgy's finest object, from his bench
- **The thunderbolt** — His masterpiece: vajra, both weapon and symbol of the awakened mind

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

mythology.body:
Tvaṣṭṛ's cycle is the Vedic meditation on craft and consequence: the hands that make the weapons, the cups, and the children are the same — and what is made can turn on its maker's world.[^1]

### Forging the Vajra (The Weapon)

When the dragon Vṛtra held the waters captive, Indra needed a weapon worthy of the deed: Tvaṣṭṛ forged the vajra, the bolt that smashed the ninety-nine fortresses and split the dragon's jaw. The Ṛgveda repeats the attribution like a signature — "the bolt that Tvaṣṭṛ made for thee" — the smith's name stamped on the pantheon's supreme weapon.[^2]

### Viśvarūpa's Three Heads (The Son)

Tvaṣṭṛ's son Viśvarūpa — three-headed, six-eyed — served as priest of the gods while secretly feeding the anti-gods' share of the offerings. Indra struck off the heads; from them sprang the partridge, the sparrow, and the quail. The smith's grief at his son's death is the hinge of the whole cycle: the forge turns from weapons for the gods to a weapon against them.

### The Making of Vṛtra (The Avenger)

Taittirīya Saṃhitā tells the terrible sequel: Tvaṣṭṛ performed a rite to create an avenger — but the accent of the mantra slipped. He meant "slayer of Indra" (indrā-śatru, with the accent of possession); the words came out "Indra-slain" — and Vṛtra, the monster he raised, was doomed by grammar to die by Indra's hand. The smith fashioned the weapon; the language fashioned the outcome.

### Saraṇyū and the Shadow (The Daughter)

His daughter Saraṇyū married the Sun and, unable to bear his blaze, left her own shadow-image in her place and fled as a mare. The Sun discovered the substitution, followed as a stallion, and of their union were born the twin Aśvins. Tvaṣṭṛ's household thus generated the gods of healing and dawn — the fashioner's line shaping light itself.

sources.citation: Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

syncretism.body:
He is India's Hephaestus in function — the lame-footed Greek smith and the Vedic fashioner are the classic comparative pair, and scholars note the shared motif of the artisan who arms both gods and their enemies. Later Hinduism merged him into Viśvakarman, "All-Maker," the architect of the universe: the Ṛgvedic name faded as the office expanded, until the carpenter's caste-god absorbed the ancient smith entirely.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], and [[kali|Kālī]].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

cultural-legacy.body: Viśvakarman Pūjā — the festival when artisans, engineers, and factory workers worship their tools — is his living descendant, kept across industrial India every September. His name survives in linguistic memory: takṣan (carpenter), and the Takṣaka serpent-lineages of epic, carry the root. The Vṛtra story's famous "accent that doomed a monster" is the standard classroom example of why the Veda guards its phonetics: in the oldest liturgy, pronunciation is destiny.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

archaeology.body: An aniconic Ṛgvedic god has no image-strata, but his craft does: the copper-bronze technology of the Harappan world — the lost-wax dancing girl, the forged tools of Chanhu-daro — is the material background of the Age in which a smith could be a god. The Viśvakarman iconography of later temple sculpture (the white-bearded architect with his tools, at Vijayanagara and across the Deccan) gives the ancient fashioner his visible afterlife.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

meditation.body:
Tvaṣṭṛ is the god of what your hands release. The bolt, the cup, the child, the monster — all leave the bench and live their own lives. His myth's terrible precision is that the rite made the weapon and the word unmade it: craft, he teaches, is only half of making; the other half is the intention the world will read in what you made.

The Vṛtra story's warning has become the engineer's daily proverb: the specification is destiny — a misplaced accent, a wrong unit, a flipped sign, and the thing built to save will kill. Tvaṣṭṛ forged perfectly and spoke imperfectly, and the monster inherited the error. Every craft since has known his double lesson: the work must be true, and the intention legible — because what we make will act on what we meant, not on what we wished we had meant.

His daughter's story completes the forge's biography: Saraṇyū, unable to bear the sun's blaze, leaves her shadow in her place — and even the fashioner's household must negotiate between the real and the shaped. From that union of truth and image come the Aśvins, the healers. The smith's line thus repairs what his own grief broke: form-giving redeemed by the medicine of his grandchildren, the forge's heat finally used to mend.

The Ṛgveda remembers him not with a temple but with an adjective: "tvaṣṭṛ-made" — the bolt, the cup, the forms of living things, all bearing the maker's mark. It is the craftsman's only immortality, and the one he would have chosen: the work outlasting the name, still doing exactly what it was fashioned to do.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

vedic-references.body:
The smith's titles follow his bench.

- **Viśvakarman** — 'All-Maker'; the later name under which the Ṛgvedic smith became the universe's architect.
- **Takṣā** — 'the Carpenter'; the craft-noun as epithet, the village trade inside the god.
- **Vajra-kartṛ** — 'Maker of the Bolt'; the hymns' signature on Indra's weapon.
- **Somapātra-kāra** — 'Fashioner of the Soma Cup'; the liturgy's finest object, attributed.
- **Viśvarūpa-janitṛ** — 'Father of Viśvarūpa'; the tragic title, the grief that drove the forge.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda 1.32, 10; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.12.

upanishads.body: Tvaṣṭṛ survives the Upanishadic abstraction as a function: the fashioning of forms becomes, in the Śvetāśvatara and the sāṃkhya-leaning texts, the self's own shaping of the body and the worlds, and the Ṛgveda's "Tvaṣṭṛ made the forms" is glossed toward the single maker. His embryonic office persists: the Kaṭha and the medical-embryological traditions keep the formation of the fetus as the divine craft par excellence, the bench-work of the form-giver under newer names.

sources.citation: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad; Ṛgveda 10.184.

puranas.body: The **Bhāgavata Purāṇa** (book 6) gives his tragedy its fullest telling: Viśvarūpa's three heads struck off by Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ's grief-driven rite, and Vṛtrāsura — the demon-son who is nobler than his killer — raised to avenge him. The Purāṇa adds the sermon the Ṛgveda withholds: Vṛtra dies as a devotee, and Indra carries the sin of priest-killing. The fashioner's story thus becomes the epic of unintended making, the Purāṇas' deepest reflection on what our works do once they leave our hands.

sources.citation: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9–12 (Vṛtrāsura cycle).

mantras.body: His living mantra is the craftsman's: **Ṛgveda 10.184** — "May Tvaṣṭṛ prepare the forms, may he make the embryo well-knit" — is recited at the garbhādhāna rite for conception, and the **Viśvakarman Sukta** (ṚV 10.81–82) hymns the All-Maker in verses the Viśvakarman Pūjā still uses: "our father, the seer, who made all things." Every September, India's workshops lay their tools before his image and the oldest smith-cult in the world takes a holiday.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda 10.184; Ṛgveda 10.81–82 (Viśvakarman Sukta).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈt̪ʋɐʂ.Ɉr̩/** — Sanskrit (IAST).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: TVASH-tuh; the ṭṛ is a rolled vocalic retroflex r.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Devanagari** — त्वष्टृ
- **Later name** — Viśvakarman
- **Owned form** — Tvaṣṭṛ

Sanskrit tvaṣṭṛ carries two retroflexes — the ṣ and the final syllabic ṛ — written त्वष्टृ in Devanagari. The name derives from the root tvakṣ, "to fashion, form," making him literally "the Fashioner": the oldest artisan theonym in the Indo-European record. Both sibilants are retroflex: tvaṣṭṛ, with the tongue curled on ṣ and the vocalic ṛ closing the name.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
